    PHC["Password Hashing Competition 2015"] --> W["Winner: Argon2"]
    W --> I["Argon2i: side-channel resistant"]
    W --> D1["Argon2d: GPU resistant"]
    W --> ID["Argon2id: hybrid, recommended default"]
    ID --> P["Tunable memory, time, parallelism"]
    O["Older options still fine: bcrypt, scrypt"] -.-> ID

prompt: A JWT (JSON Web Token) typically consists of three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots. What are they, in order?
options: key.certificate.chain
request.response.status
subject.issuer.audience
header.payload.signature
optionNotes: Key, certificate, and chain are components of a TLS/X.509 setup, not the segments of a JWT.
Request, response, and status are HTTP concepts and have no relation to the structure of a token.
`sub`, `iss`, and `aud` are registered claim names that live inside the payload; they are not the three top-level segments.
Header (algorithm and type), payload (claims), and signature (integrity check over the first two) are the three dot-separated parts of a compact JWT.
explanation: A compact JWT has three dot-separated segments: a header (algorithm/type metadata), a payload (the claims), and a signature that lets a verifier check the token's integrity.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    J["JWT: xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz"] --> H["1. Header: alg HS256, typ JWT"]
    J --> P["2. Payload: claims like sub, exp"]
    J --> S["3. Signature: HMAC(header.payload, secret)"]
    H --> V["Verifier recomputes signature"]
    P --> V
    S --> V
    V --> R["Integrity confirmed"]

prompt: By default, the payload (claims) of a standard signed JWT (JWS) is encrypted and unreadable to anyone who does not hold the signing key.
explanation: The payload is only base64url-*encoded*, not encrypted — anyone holding the token can decode and read it. The signature only protects integrity, not confidentiality, so sensitive data shouldn't be placed in a plain JWT payload unless it is separately encrypted (e.g., using JWE).
example:
# Anyone with the token can read the claims without any key
echo 'eyJzdWIiOiJhbGljZSIsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9' | base64 -d
# {"sub":"alice","role":"admin"}
# The signature only proves integrity; use JWE if claims must stay confidential
diagram:
flowchart LR
    T["Signed JWT (JWS)"] --> P["Payload: base64url encoded"]
    P -->|"base64 -d, no key"| R["Anyone can read the claims"]
    T --> S["Signature: protects integrity only"]
    S -.->|"does NOT hide content"| R
    N["Need confidentiality?"] --> E["Use JWE (encrypted JWT)"]

prompt: What problem does CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) solve?
options: It provides a browser-enforced, header-based mechanism that lets a server explicitly allow specific other origins to make requests to its resources, relaxing the default same-origin policy
It unconditionally blocks every cross-origin request
It replaces the need for authentication tokens entirely
It encrypts traffic exchanged between two different origins
optionNotes: A browser-enforced, header-based protocol that lets a server explicitly allow specific foreign origins, relaxing the same-origin policy, is exactly what CORS is.
The same-origin policy is what restricts cross-origin reads by default; CORS is the mechanism to selectively permit them, not to block everything.
CORS only governs which origins a browser may read responses from; requests still need normal authentication such as tokens or cookies.
Encryption of traffic is provided by TLS; CORS headers are plain metadata about permitted origins and do not encrypt anything.
explanation: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy by default. CORS is the opt-in, header-based protocol (e.g., `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`) that lets a server relax that restriction for specific origins it trusts.
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as "Browser at app.example.com"
    participant A as "api.example.org"
    Note over B: same-origin policy blocks cross-origin reads by default
    B->>A: OPTIONS preflight with Origin header
    A-->>B: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
    B->>A: GET /data
    A-->>B: Response, browser allows JS to read it
    Note over B,A: Server opts in to specific trusted origins

prompt: What best describes a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attack?
options: An attacker injects malicious JavaScript that later executes in victims' browsers
An attacker tricks a logged-in victim's browser into unknowingly submitting a request to a site where the victim is authenticated, relying on cookies the browser attaches automatically
An attacker floods a server with traffic to exhaust its resources
An attacker repeatedly guesses a user's password through a login form
optionNotes: Injecting JavaScript that runs in other users' browsers is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), a different attack class.
Tricking an authenticated victim's browser into sending a state-changing request the victim did not intend, relying on automatically attached cookies, is the definition of CSRF.
Flooding a server to exhaust resources is a denial-of-service attack.
Repeated password guessing through a login form is a brute-force attack, not request forgery.
explanation: CSRF exploits the browser's automatic inclusion of credentials (like session cookies) on requests: a malicious page can cause the victim's browser to submit a state-changing request to another site the victim is already authenticated to, without the victim's knowledge.
example:
# Attack shape (defensive illustration): a hidden form on evil.example auto-submits to the bank
# <form action="https://bank.example/transfer" method="POST"> ... </form>
# The browser attaches the bank's session cookie automatically.
# Defense: bank sets
Set-Cookie: session=...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
# and requires a per-session CSRF token in every POST
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as "Victim browser"
    participant E as "evil.example"
    participant B as "bank.example"
    Note over V,B: Victim already logged in, session cookie set
    V->>E: Visit malicious page
    E-->>V: Hidden form auto-submits to bank
    V->>B: POST /transfer (cookie attached automatically)
    B-->>V: Transfer executed as the victim

prompt: Which of the following are effective mitigations against CSRF attacks?
options: Using anti-CSRF (synchronizer) tokens that must be included in state-changing requests
Setting the `SameSite` attribute on session cookies to `Lax` or `Strict`
Disabling TLS to simplify how requests are handled
Validating the `Origin` or `Referer` header on sensitive requests
Increasing the session cookie's expiration time to 30 days
optionNotes: Synchronizer tokens are unpredictable per-session values that a forging site cannot know, so requests without a valid token are rejected.
The `SameSite` cookie attribute set to `Lax` or `Strict` tells browsers not to attach the cookie on most or all cross-site requests, removing the ambient credential CSRF relies on.
Disabling TLS removes transport protection and does nothing to stop forged requests; it weakens security overall.
Checking the `Origin` or `Referer` header lets the server reject state-changing requests that originate from an unexpected site.
A longer cookie lifetime keeps the session valid longer, which if anything widens the window for CSRF rather than mitigating it.
explanation: CSRF tokens, the `SameSite` cookie attribute, and Origin/Referer validation are all standard, effective CSRF defenses. Disabling TLS removes an unrelated protection and weakens security, and lengthening cookie lifetime does nothing to stop CSRF.
example:
# Django enables all three defenses with a few settings
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = True
SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax"       # SameSite attribute
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = ["https://app.example.com"]   # Origin/Referer check
# Template: <form method="post">{% csrf_token %} ...   # synchronizer token
diagram:
flowchart TD
    C["CSRF request from evil.example"] --> M["Mitigations"]
    M --> T["Anti-CSRF synchronizer token required in form"]
    M --> S["Cookie SameSite=Lax or Strict: cookie not sent cross-site"]
    M --> O["Validate Origin or Referer header"]
    T --> X["Forged request rejected"]
    S --> X
    O --> X

prompt: Which HTTP response header instructs browsers to only ever connect to a site over HTTPS, even if the user types `http://` or follows an HTTP link?
explanation: The `Strict-Transport-Security` header (commonly abbreviated HSTS) tells a compliant browser to automatically upgrade future requests to that host to HTTPS, helping prevent protocol-downgrade and cookie-hijacking attacks.
example:
# nginx: tell browsers to use HTTPS only for the next year, including subdomains
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload" always;
# Verify
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i strict-transport
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as "Browser"
    participant S as "example.com"
    B->>S: First HTTPS visit
    S-->>B: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
    B->>B: Remember: HTTPS only for this host
    Note over B: User types http://example.com
    B->>S: Auto-upgraded to https:// before sending
    Note over B,S: Blocks downgrade and cookie hijack

prompt: What does the `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header prevent?
options: Pages from being rendered on mobile browsers
The server from logging incoming requests
Browsers from MIME-sniffing a response into a different content type than the server declared, which can prevent certain content-type-confusion attacks
Cookies from ever being sent on cross-site requests
optionNotes: Rendering on mobile browsers is unaffected; this header has nothing to do with device or viewport handling.
Server-side request logging is configured in the web server; a response header sent to clients does not control it.
Telling browsers not to MIME-sniff and to honor the declared `Content-Type` is exactly what `nosniff` does, blocking content-type confusion tricks.
Restricting cookies on cross-site requests is done with the `SameSite` cookie attribute, not with `X-Content-Type-Options`.
explanation: Without `nosniff`, some browsers try to guess a resource's type from its content rather than trusting the declared `Content-Type`, which attackers have abused to get a file treated as executable script; `nosniff` disables that guessing.
example:
# Serve every response with nosniff so browsers honor the declared Content-Type
add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
# Without it, a user-uploaded 'image' containing JS might be executed as a script
curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i x-content-type
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["User uploads file declared as text/plain"] --> S["Server: Content-Type: text/plain"]
    S --> B{"Browser MIME sniffing?"}
    B -->|"no nosniff header"| G["Browser guesses: looks like JavaScript, executes it"]
    B -->|"X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff"| T["Browser trusts declared type, no execution"]
    G --> X["Content-type confusion attack"]

prompt: Which of the following HTTP response headers help improve a web application's security posture?
options: `Content-Security-Policy`
`Strict-Transport-Security`
`X-Content-Type-Options`
`Content-Length`
`Accept-Language`
optionNotes: `Content-Security-Policy` restricts which sources scripts, styles, and other resources may load from, which is a primary defense against XSS.
`Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS) forces browsers to use HTTPS for the host, defeating protocol downgrade and cookie-stripping attacks.
`X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` stops browsers from guessing a different MIME type than the one declared, preventing content-type confusion.
`Content-Length` simply states the size of the response body in bytes and has no security role.
`Accept-Language` is a request header the browser sends to indicate preferred languages; it is not a response header and has no security purpose.
explanation: CSP, HSTS, and X-Content-Type-Options are all security-focused response headers. `Content-Length` and `Accept-Language` are ordinary functional headers with no direct security purpose.
diagram:
flowchart TD
    H["Security response headers"] --> CSP["Content-Security-Policy: limits script sources"]
    H --> HSTS["Strict-Transport-Security: HTTPS only"]
    H --> X["X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff"]
    F["Functional headers, no security role"] --> CL["Content-Length"]
    F --> AL["Accept-Language"]

prompt: What is Open Policy Agent (OPA) primarily used for?
options: It is a secrets manager comparable to Vault
It is a certificate authority that issues TLS certificates
It is a container runtime, similar to containerd

It is a general-purpose policy engine that lets teams define and enforce policies as code — for example, Kubernetes admission control, service authorization, or CI/CD checks — decoupled from the services that enforce them
optionNotes: Secrets management is Vault's domain; OPA stores and evaluates policy, not credentials.
Issuing TLS certificates is what a CA such as cert-manager with Let's Encrypt or Fulcio does; OPA makes allow/deny decisions.
Container runtimes such as containerd or CRI-O execute containers; OPA does not run workloads.

A general-purpose policy engine that evaluates policy-as-code from many enforcement points (Kubernetes admission via Gatekeeper, API gateways, CI checks) while staying decoupled from the services is exactly what OPA is.
explanation: OPA is a standalone, general-purpose policy engine: you author policies once and evaluate them from many different enforcement points (Kubernetes via Gatekeeper, API gateways, CI pipelines, etc.), keeping policy logic out of application code.

prompt: You must apply a NetworkPolicy in namespace `prod` that blocks all ingress and egress traffic to every Pod in that namespace, so that teams then add explicit allow rules. Which manifest fragment achieves a full default deny?
options: `spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]}` with no `ingress` or `egress` rules
`spec: {podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress]}` with an empty `ingress: [{}]` rule
`spec: {podSelector: {matchLabels: {deny: "all"}}, policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]}`
`spec: {podSelector: {}}` with `ingress: [{}]` and `egress: [{}]`
optionNotes: An empty `podSelector` selects every Pod in the namespace, and listing both `Ingress` and `Egress` in `policyTypes` with no rules means nothing is allowed in either direction, which is the standard default-deny pattern.
`ingress: [{}]` is a rule that matches all sources, so this actually allows all ingress; egress is not covered at all because it is not listed in `policyTypes`.
This only selects Pods carrying the label `deny=all`; Pods without that label are unaffected and remain fully open.
Without `policyTypes`, `Egress` is only inferred when an `egress` section exists, and `ingress: [{}]` / `egress: [{}]` are allow-all rules, so this permits all traffic rather than denying it.
explanation: A default-deny policy uses an empty `podSelector` (all Pods in the namespace) and declares both `Ingress` and `Egress` in `policyTypes` while providing no rules, so no traffic matches an allow. An empty rule object `{}` is the opposite: it matches everything and therefore allows all traffic. Label-scoped selectors leave unlabeled Pods unprotected.
example:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}        # every Pod in prod
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress               # no rules listed -> nothing allowed

    P -->|"egress blocked"| DST["Any destination"]
    NP["NetworkPolicy podSelector empty"] --> P
    NP --> T["policyTypes Ingress and Egress"]
    ALLOW["Additional allow policies"] -->|"punch holes"| P

prompt: If a ServiceAccount has `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, a Pod using that ServiceAccount can still get a token mounted by setting `automountServiceAccountToken: true` in its own Pod spec.
explanation: The Pod-level `automountServiceAccountToken` field takes precedence over the ServiceAccount-level setting, so a Pod can opt back in even when the ServiceAccount disables mounting.   name: app

  name: needs-api
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app
  automountServiceAccountToken: true  # Pod-level wins

prompt: During a hardening review you run `curl -k https://<control-plane>:6443/api` without credentials and receive a `403 Forbidden` for user `system:anonymous` rather than `401 Unauthorized`. Which kube-apiserver flag change makes unauthenticated requests be rejected outright at the authentication stage?
options: `--anonymous-auth=false`
`--authorization-mode=RBAC`
`--insecure-port=0`
`--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction`
optionNotes: `--anonymous-auth=false` stops the API server from mapping unauthenticated requests to `system:anonymous`, so they fail authentication with `401` instead of reaching authorization. This is the CIS-recommended setting.
RBAC is already what produced the `403`: the anonymous user was authenticated and then denied. Changing the authorizer does not stop the anonymous identity from being created.
The insecure port was removed in Kubernetes 1.20 and this flag no longer exists; it would have addressed an unauthenticated HTTP listener, not anonymous requests on 6443.
`NodeRestriction` is an admission plugin that limits what kubelets can modify; admission runs after authentication and authorization and does not affect anonymous access.
explanation: A `403` for `system:anonymous` shows anonymous authentication is enabled: the request was authenticated as the anonymous user and then rejected by RBAC. Setting `--anonymous-auth=false` rejects such requests at the authentication step. Note that some health endpoints need anonymous access for probes, so review liveness configuration before changing it in production.
example:
# /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - command:
    - kube-apiserver
    - --anonymous-auth=false          # reject unauthenticated requests
    - --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC
# verify
curl -k https://10.0.0.10:6443/api   # now 401 Unauthorized
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["Unauthenticated request"] --> A{"anonymous-auth?"}
    A -->|"true"| U["user system:anonymous"]
    U --> Z["RBAC authorization"]
    Z --> F["403 Forbidden"]
    A -->|"false"| R["401 Unauthorized"]

prompt: You want to confine a container with a custom AppArmor profile named `k8s-deny-write`. Which statements about doing this on a current Kubernetes cluster are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: The profile must already be loaded into the kernel on every node where the Pod may be scheduled, for example with `apparmor_parser`.
The profile is referenced in `securityContext.appArmorProfile` with `type: Localhost` and `localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write`.
Kubernetes automatically distributes the profile file to nodes when the Pod is created.
If the node does not have the profile loaded, the Pod is rejected or stays blocked rather than running unconfined.
AppArmor profiles are applied through the `seccompProfile` field with `type: AppArmor`.
optionNotes: Correct: Kubernetes only references profiles by name; loading them onto each node is an operator responsibility, typically done with `apparmor_parser -r` or a DaemonSet.
Correct: since v1.30 the `appArmorProfile` field in the Pod or container `securityContext` (GA) replaces the older `container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<name>` annotation.
Incorrect: Kubernetes has no mechanism to ship AppArmor profiles to nodes; it only asks the container runtime to apply an already-loaded profile.
Correct: the kubelet validates that the profile exists; if it does not, the Pod fails to start rather than silently running unconfined.
Incorrect: `seccompProfile` configures seccomp syscall filtering, a different Linux security module; AppArmor uses its own `appArmorProfile` field.
explanation: AppArmor confinement works only when the named profile is loaded in the node kernel; Kubernetes then references it through `securityContext.appArmorProfile` (GA in v1.30, replacing the beta annotation). The kubelet refuses to run a container whose profile is missing. Seccomp is a separate mechanism with its own field.
example:
# on each node
sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/k8s-deny-write
sudo aa-status | grep k8s-deny-write
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hello
spec:
  securityContext:
    appArmorProfile:
      type: Localhost
      localhostProfile: k8s-deny-write
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: ["sh","-c","touch /tmp/x || echo denied; sleep 3600"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    OP["Operator loads profile with apparmor_parser"] --> K["Node kernel has k8s-deny-write"]
    POD["Pod securityContext appArmorProfile Localhost"] --> KL["kubelet validates profile exists"]
    KL -->|"found"| RT["Runtime applies profile to container"]
    KL -->|"missing"| ERR["Pod fails to start"]
    K --> KL

prompt: In a Pod or container `securityContext`, what value of `seccompProfile.type` applies the container runtime's built-in default seccomp profile, as required by the `restricted` Pod Security Standard?
explanation: `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` tells the kubelet to apply the container runtime's default seccomp profile (for example containerd's), which blocks dangerous syscalls such as `reboot` and `mount`. `Localhost` references a custom profile file under the kubelet seccomp directory, and `Unconfined` disables filtering. The `restricted` PSS level requires `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`.
example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: audited
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault    # runtime's default syscall allowlist
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:1.27
diagram:
flowchart LR
    SC["securityContext.seccompProfile.type"] --> RD["RuntimeDefault - runtime default profile"]
    SC --> LH["Localhost - custom JSON on node"]
    SC --> UC["Unconfined - no filtering"]
    RD --> OK["Allowed by restricted PSS"]
    LH --> OK
    UC --> NO["Rejected by restricted PSS"]

prompt: A namespace carries the labels `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline`, `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted` and `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted`. A user applies a Pod that runs as root but does not use host namespaces or privileged mode. What happens?
options: The Pod is created, the user sees a warning in kubectl output, and an audit annotation is recorded
The Pod is rejected because it violates the restricted level
The Pod is created silently because baseline is satisfied
The Pod is rejected because audit mode logs and blocks the request
optionNotes: Correct: running as root is allowed by `baseline`, so `enforce` passes; but it violates `restricted`, so the `warn` mode returns a client-side warning and `audit` mode adds an annotation to the audit log entry. Neither of those modes blocks.
Only the `enforce` mode can reject Pods, and it is set to `baseline`, which permits running as root.
`warn` and `audit` are evaluated against `restricted`, which the Pod fails, so the creation is not silent.
`audit` mode never blocks; it only records a `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-violations` annotation in the audit event.
explanation: Pod Security Admission evaluates each mode independently against its own level. `enforce` is the only mode that rejects; `warn` returns a warning to the client and `audit` annotates the audit log. Because root is permitted by `baseline` but forbidden by `restricted`, the Pod is admitted with a warning and an audit annotation, a common pattern for previewing a stricter policy before enforcing it.
example:
kubectl label ns dev \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted
kubectl run root -n dev --image=nginx
# Warning: would violate PodSecurity "restricted:latest": runAsNonRoot != true ...
# pod/root created

prompt: You add an `EncryptionConfiguration` with an `aescbc` provider listed first and `identity` second, restart kube-apiserver, and then read a Secret directly from etcd with `etcdctl get` but it is still plaintext. Why, and what fixes it?
options: Existing Secrets are only encrypted when written; run `kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -` to rewrite them
The `identity` provider must be listed first so reads succeed; reorder the providers and restart
The API server ignores `EncryptionConfiguration` until the `--encryption-provider-config-automatic-reload` flag is set
The Secret is encrypted; `etcdctl` transparently decrypts values using the API server's key
optionNotes: Correct: the first provider is used to encrypt new writes, but data already in etcd stays in whatever form it was stored; a rewrite of every Secret forces it through the encrypting provider.
Listing `identity` first would make the API server write plaintext; `identity` is placed last precisely so that old unencrypted data can still be read while new writes are encrypted.
That flag only lets the API server reload a changed config without restart; the configuration is active as soon as `--encryption-provider-config` points at the file.
`etcdctl` talks directly to etcd and has no access to the API server's encryption keys; encrypted values appear with a `k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:` prefix.
explanation: Encryption at rest is applied on write. The first provider in the list encrypts new data, and every listed provider is tried in order when reading, which is why `identity` goes last to keep legacy plaintext readable. To encrypt pre-existing Secrets you must rewrite them, after which `etcdctl` shows the `k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:` prefix instead of plaintext.
example:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
- resources: [secrets]
  providers:
  - aescbc:
      keys:
      - name: key1
        secret: <base64 32-byte key>
  - identity: {}          # read old plaintext, never first
# after restart, re-encrypt existing data
kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
diagram:
flowchart LR
    W["Write Secret"] --> P1["Provider 1 aescbc encrypts"]
    P1 --> E["etcd value k8s:enc:aescbc:v1"]
    R["Read Secret"] --> T["Try providers in order"]
    T --> P1
    T --> ID["identity reads legacy plaintext"]
    OLD["Pre-existing plaintext"] -->|"kubectl replace"| W

prompt: You configure the `ImagePolicyWebhook` admission controller with `defaultAllow: false` in its `imagePolicy` configuration. During an incident the external image policy backend becomes unreachable. What is the effect on new Pod creations?
options: All new Pods are rejected until the backend is reachable again
All new Pods are admitted because the webhook fails open
Only Pods using images with mutable tags are rejected
Pods are admitted but flagged with an `imagepolicy.k8s.io/failed-open` annotation
optionNotes: Correct: `defaultAllow: false` means that when the backend cannot be contacted (or returns an error), the admission decision defaults to deny, so Pod creation fails closed.
Failing open is the behaviour of `defaultAllow: true`; it prioritises availability over enforcement and is the setting the question rules out.
The webhook does not inspect tag mutability itself; it forwards the image references to the backend, and with no backend there is no per-image decision.
`failed-open` annotations are added only when `defaultAllow: true` lets a request through after a backend failure.
explanation: The `ImagePolicyWebhook` plugin sends an `ImageReview` to an external service for every Pod. `defaultAllow` decides what happens when that service is unavailable: `false` fails closed and blocks Pods, `true` fails open and admits them with an annotation. Choosing `false` is safer for supply-chain enforcement but makes the backend a hard availability dependency.
example:
# admission configuration file passed via --admission-control-config-file
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AdmissionConfiguration
plugins:
- name: ImagePolicyWebhook
  configuration:
    imagePolicy:
      kubeConfigFile: /etc/kubernetes/imagepolicy/kubeconfig.yaml
      allowTTL: 50
      denyTTL: 50
      retryBackoff: 500
      defaultAllow: false     # fail closed when backend is down
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["kubectl create pod"] --> API["kube-apiserver admission"]
    API --> W["ImagePolicyWebhook"]
    W -->|"ImageReview"| B["External policy backend"]
    B -->|"allowed true"| OK["Pod created"]
    B -->|"allowed false"| NO["Pod rejected"]
    W -->|"backend unreachable and defaultAllow false"| NO

prompt: You are writing a kube-apiserver audit `Policy`. For Secret writes you want the event to include the request metadata and the request body, but you do not want the response body stored. Which audit `level` should the rule use?
options: `Request`
`RequestResponse`
`Metadata`
`None`
optionNotes: Correct: `Request` logs event metadata plus the request body but omits the response body; it is the highest level that still keeps the returned object out of the log.
`RequestResponse` logs metadata, request body and response body, so the returned Secret contents would be written to the audit log.
`Metadata` records only who did what to which resource (user, verb, resource, timestamp) without any request body.
`None` disables logging for matching requests entirely.
explanation: Audit rules are matched top to bottom and the first matching rule sets the level. The four levels are cumulative: `None`, `Metadata`, `Request` (adds request body) and `RequestResponse` (adds response body as well). For sensitive kinds like Secrets, `Metadata` is the common recommendation; if you need the request body, `Request` is the highest level that avoids persisting the response.
example:
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
- level: Request              # metadata + request body, no response
  resources:
  - group: ""
    resources: ["secrets"]
  verbs: ["create","update","patch","delete"]
- level: Metadata
  omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    N["None - nothing"] --> M["Metadata - user verb resource"]
    M --> R["Request - plus request body"]
    R --> RR["RequestResponse - plus response body"]
    S["Stages RequestReceived ResponseStarted ResponseComplete Panic"] --> M

prompt: The '4Cs of Cloud Native Security' model describes security as layered. Ordered from the outermost layer to the innermost, what are the four layers?
options: Cloud, Cluster, Container, Code
Code, Container, Cluster, Cloud
Cloud, Cluster, Code, Container
Compliance, Cluster, Container, Code
optionNotes: Correct: the cloud (or datacenter) is the outermost layer, the cluster sits inside it, containers run inside the cluster, and application code is innermost; each layer relies on the security of the layer outside it.
This is the correct set of layers but reversed; the model is presented from the outside in, with Code as the innermost layer.
Container sits between Cluster and Code; the container image and runtime configuration protect the code running inside.
Compliance is not one of the 4Cs; the outermost layer is the Cloud or infrastructure provider.
explanation: The 4Cs model is Cloud, Cluster, Container and Code, from outer to inner. Its key message is that each inner layer inherits the weaknesses of the layers around it: strong application code cannot compensate for a cluster whose API server is exposed, or a cloud account with over-permissive IAM.
example:
# one control per layer
Cloud:     restrict API server access to a private CIDR
Cluster:   RBAC + Pod Security Admission + NetworkPolicy
Container: scan images, run as non-root, drop capabilities
Code:      dependency scanning, TLS, input validation
diagram:
flowchart TD
    CL["Cloud - provider IAM network"] --> CU["Cluster - API server RBAC policies"]
    CU --> CO["Container - images runtime settings"]
    CO --> CD["Code - application and dependencies"]
    CD -.->|"depends on outer layers"| CL

prompt: In a STRIDE threat model of a Kubernetes cluster, an attacker who captures a ServiceAccount token from a compromised Pod and uses it to make API requests as that ServiceAccount is exploiting which threat category?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Denial of Service
optionNotes: Correct: Spoofing is impersonating another identity; presenting a stolen credential to act as the ServiceAccount is textbook identity spoofing.
Tampering is unauthorised modification of data or code, such as altering etcd contents or an image in a registry; reusing a token does not itself modify anything.
Repudiation is the ability to deny having performed an action, typically due to missing audit logs; it is a consequence that could follow but not the category of the attack.
Denial of Service concerns exhausting resources or availability, which is not the goal of token replay.
explanation: STRIDE classifies threats as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. Using a stolen token to act as another principal is Spoofing. Kubernetes mitigations include short-lived projected tokens, `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, and least-privilege RBAC so a stolen token has limited value.
example:
# attacker inside a compromised Pod
TOKEN=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/prod/secrets
# API server sees the request as the ServiceAccount, not the attacker
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Attacker in compromised Pod"] -->|"reads token file"| T["ServiceAccount token"]
    A -->|"presents token"| API["API server"]
    API -->|"authenticates as SA"| S["Spoofing"]
    M["Mitigations short-lived tokens least privilege RBAC"] --> API

prompt: A request to the Kubernetes API server passes through three security stages before the object is persisted to etcd. In what order are they evaluated?
options: Authentication, authorization, admission control
Admission control, authentication, authorization
Authorization, authentication, admission control
Authentication, admission control, authorization
optionNotes: Correct: the API server first establishes who is calling (authentication), then whether that identity may perform the verb on the resource (authorization), and finally runs mutating and validating admission plugins on the request content.
Admission control needs to know the authenticated user and only runs on requests that are already authorized, so it cannot come first.
Authorization decisions are made about an identity, so authentication must happen before authorization.
Admission plugins run after authorization; an unauthorized request is rejected before any admission webhook is called.
explanation: Every API request is authenticated (certificates, tokens, OIDC), then authorized (RBAC, Node, Webhook), then passed through admission control (mutating, then validating) before being written to etcd. Failing any stage rejects the request, and admission control only applies to requests that create, modify or delete objects.
example:
kubectl auth whoami                              # authentication result
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n prod           # authorization check
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations      # admission stage
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["Request"] --> AN["Authentication - who are you"]
    AN --> AZ["Authorization - may you do this"]
    AZ --> MA["Mutating admission"]
    MA --> VA["Validating admission"]
    VA --> E["Persist to etcd"]

prompt: The `baseline` Pod Security Standard allows a Pod to use `hostNetwork: true` as long as it does not run in privileged mode.
explanation: The `baseline` level forbids sharing host namespaces, so `hostNetwork`, `hostPID` and `hostIPC` must all be unset or false, along with privileged containers, most added capabilities, hostPath volumes and hostPorts. Only the `privileged` level is unrestricted. `restricted` builds on `baseline` by additionally requiring non-root, dropping all capabilities and a seccomp profile.
example:
# rejected in a namespace with enforce=baseline
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sniffer
spec:
  hostNetwork: true      # host namespace -> violates baseline
  containers:
  - name: tcpdump
    image: nicolaka/netshoot
diagram:
flowchart TD
    PR["privileged - no restrictions"] --> BL["baseline - no host namespaces no privileged no hostPath"]
    BL --> RS["restricted - plus non-root drop ALL seccomp"]
    HN["hostNetwork true"] -->|"allowed only at"| PR

prompt: Which statements about workload isolation techniques in Kubernetes are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
options: Namespaces alone do not prevent Pods in different namespaces from communicating over the network.
Sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers reduce the attack surface of the shared host kernel.
Placing sensitive workloads on dedicated nodes via taints and node affinity is a form of physical isolation.
Creating a separate namespace automatically gives its Pods a separate kernel.
A NetworkPolicy applied in one namespace blocks traffic for all namespaces in the cluster.
optionNotes: Correct: namespaces are a logical scoping mechanism for names, RBAC and quotas; without NetworkPolicy, cross-namespace traffic is allowed.
Correct: gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel and Kata runs each Pod in a lightweight VM, so a container escape does not directly reach the host kernel.
Correct: node-level isolation ensures multi-tenant or untrusted workloads never share a kernel with sensitive ones, complementing logical controls.
Incorrect: all containers on a node share that node's kernel regardless of namespace; only sandboxing or separate nodes change the kernel boundary.
Incorrect: NetworkPolicy is namespaced and only affects Pods selected within its own namespace.
explanation: Isolation in Kubernetes is layered: namespaces provide logical separation, NetworkPolicy provides network segmentation within the namespace it lives in, sandboxed runtimes isolate the kernel boundary, and dedicated nodes provide hardware-level separation. Namespaces never change the shared-kernel model on their own.
example:
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc            # sandboxed runtime
---
# Pod opts in and is pinned to hardened nodes
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  nodeSelector:
    tier: sensitive
  tolerations:
  - key: sensitive
    operator: Exists
diagram:
flowchart TD
    L["Isolation layers"] --> NS["Namespace - names RBAC quotas"]
    L --> NP["NetworkPolicy - segmentation"]
    L --> SB["Sandbox - gVisor Kata kernel boundary"]
    L --> ND["Dedicated nodes - taints affinity"]
    NS -.->|"does not isolate"| K["Shared host kernel"]
    SB -->|"isolates"| K

prompt: A security team wants a reference that catalogues real-world adversary tactics and techniques specific to containers, such as 'Deploy Container' for execution or 'Escape to Host' for privilege escalation, to map detections against. Which framework is this?
options: MITRE ATT&CK Containers matrix
CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
NIST SP 800-190
PCI DSS
optionNotes: Correct: the ATT&CK Containers matrix organises observed attacker behaviour into tactics (Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation and so on) and techniques, which teams use to assess detection coverage.
The CIS Benchmark is a prescriptive checklist of configuration hardening controls with pass/fail checks, not a catalogue of attacker techniques.
NIST SP 800-190 is the Application Container Security Guide, a set of risk descriptions and countermeasure recommendations rather than a tactic/technique matrix.
PCI DSS is a compliance standard for organisations handling payment card data; it defines requirements, not adversary behaviour.
explanation: MITRE ATT&CK is a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques; its Containers matrix covers orchestration and container-level attacks. CIS Benchmarks and NIST SP 800-190 describe how to configure and secure systems, and PCI DSS is a regulatory compliance standard. Teams often combine them: harden with CIS, assess risk with NIST, and validate detections against ATT&CK.
example:
# example Falco rule mapped to ATT&CK technique
- rule: Container Escape via Mount
  desc: Detect mount syscall from a container (T1611 Escape to Host)
  condition: container and evt.type = mount
  output: "Mount in container (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, mitre_privilege_escalation, T1611]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["MITRE ATT&CK Containers"] --> T1["Initial Access - exposed dashboard"]
    A --> T2["Execution - deploy container"]
    A --> T3["Privilege Escalation - escape to host"]
    A --> T4["Credential Access - steal tokens"]

- --audit-log-maxage=30
- --audit-log-maxbackup=10
# and matching volumeMounts / hostPath volumes

prompt: With a default Kubernetes installation and no additional configuration, how are `Secret` objects stored in etcd?
options: Base64-encoded but not encrypted, readable by anyone with etcd or broad API access
Encrypted with AES using a key generated automatically by kubeadm
Encrypted using each node's kubelet client certificate
Stored only in memory on the API server and never written to etcd
optionNotes: Correct: by default Secret values are base64-encoded (an encoding, not encryption) and written to etcd as-is, so etcd access, backups and over-broad RBAC all expose them; encryption at rest must be configured explicitly.
No encryption key is generated by default; enabling encryption at rest requires an `EncryptionConfiguration` supplied to the API server.
Kubelet certificates authenticate nodes to the API server; they play no role in storing Secrets.
Secrets are persisted in etcd like any other object; the in-memory behaviour is a property of tmpfs mounts on nodes, not of storage.
explanation: Kubernetes Secrets are a separate object type mainly so RBAC can restrict them, but by default they sit in etcd unencrypted. Good practice is to enable encryption at rest (ideally with a KMS provider), restrict `get`/`list` on Secrets via RBAC, protect etcd and its backups, and consider an external secret manager for high-value credentials.
example:
# what etcd holds by default
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/default/db-pass \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key | strings
# ... password=hunter2   <- plaintext
diagram:
flowchart LR
    S["Secret manifest base64 values"] --> API["API server"]
    API -->|"default no encryption"| E["etcd plaintext"]
    API -->|"with EncryptionConfiguration"| EE["etcd ciphertext"]
    B["etcd backups"] --- E
    R["RBAC on secrets"] --> API
    X["External secret manager"] -.-> API

prompt: In Kyverno, what is the difference between a `ClusterPolicy` and a `Policy`?
options: `ClusterPolicy` is cluster-scoped and applies to resources in any namespace; `Policy` is namespaced and applies only to resources in its own namespace
`ClusterPolicy` can only contain validate rules; `Policy` can also contain mutate and generate rules
`ClusterPolicy` is evaluated by the admission webhook; `Policy` is only evaluated by background scans
`Policy` is the legacy v1 kind and `ClusterPolicy` replaced it in Kyverno 1.10
optionNotes: Correct: the two kinds share the same spec; the only difference is scope. A `ClusterPolicy` matches across all namespaces (and cluster-scoped resources), while a `Policy` lives in a namespace and only affects resources there, making it suitable for tenant self-service.
Both kinds support all rule types; the rule types are not tied to scope.
Both are enforced at admission and both can be background-scanned.
Both kinds exist in the current `kyverno.io/v1` API and neither is deprecated.
explanation: `ClusterPolicy` and `Policy` are identical in structure and capability; the difference is scope. Cluster administrators typically use `ClusterPolicy` for organisation-wide guardrails, while namespaced `Policy` resources let teams add their own rules without cluster-wide permissions. Namespaced policies cannot match cluster-scoped resources.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: Policy                 # namespaced
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
  namespace: team-a          # only affects team-a
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-team
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Deployment]
    validate:
      message: "team label is required"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          labels:
            team: "?*"
diagram:
flowchart TD
    CP["ClusterPolicy"] --> N1["namespace a"]
    CP --> N2["namespace b"]
    CP --> CS["cluster-scoped resources"]
    P["Policy in namespace a"] --> N1
    P -.->|"cannot reach"| N2

prompt: Which of these are rule types you can declare inside a Kyverno `ClusterPolicy` rule? (Select all that apply.)
options: `validate`
`mutate`
`verifyImages`
`enforce`
`audit`
`alert`
optionNotes: Correct: `validate` checks resources against a pattern, deny conditions or CEL expressions.
Correct: `mutate` modifies resources at admission or on existing resources, using strategic merge or JSON patches.
Correct: `verifyImages` checks container image signatures and attestations, typically with cosign or notary.
Incorrect: `Enforce` is a value of `validationFailureAction`, not a rule type.
Incorrect: `Audit` is the other `validationFailureAction` value; it controls whether validate failures block or only report.
Incorrect: Kyverno has no `alert` rule type; alerting is done from PolicyReports by external tooling.
explanation: A Kyverno rule declares exactly one of `validate`, `mutate`, `generate`, `verifyImages` or (in `CleanupPolicy` resources) cleanup behaviour. `Enforce` and `Audit` are values for `validationFailureAction`, which decides whether a failing validate rule blocks the request or just records a report entry.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["Kyverno rule"] --> V["validate"]
    R --> M["mutate"]
    R --> G["generate"]
    R --> VI["verifyImages"]
    CP["CleanupPolicy"] --> CL["cleanup"]
    V --> FA["validationFailureAction Enforce or Audit"]

prompt: A Kyverno validate rule with `validationFailureAction: Audit` blocks admission of any resource that fails the rule and records the failure in a PolicyReport.
explanation: `Audit` mode never blocks: the resource is admitted and the violation is recorded as a `fail` result in a PolicyReport (and as a warning in the API response). Only `Enforce` rejects the request. Teams typically roll out new policies in `Audit`, review the reports, then switch to `Enforce`.
example:
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Audit   # admit, but report
  rules:
  - name: require-requests
    match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}]}
    validate:
      message: "CPU and memory requests are required"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - resources:
              requests:
                cpu: "?*"
                memory: "?*"
# kubectl get policyreport -A   -> shows FAIL entries
diagram:
flowchart TD
    REQ["Resource fails validate rule"] --> A{"validationFailureAction"}
    A -->|"Enforce"| DENY["Request rejected"]
    A -->|"Audit"| ADMIT["Request admitted"]
    ADMIT --> PR["PolicyReport fail entry"]
    ADMIT --> W["Warning to client"]

prompt: You need a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that validates every Deployment in the cluster except those in the `kube-system` and `kyverno` namespaces. How should the rule's selection be written?
options: `match.any[].resources.kinds: [Deployment]` plus `exclude.any[].resources.namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno]`
`match.any[].resources.kinds: [Deployment]` plus `match.any[].resources.namespaces: ["!kube-system", "!kyverno"]`
Two separate `match` blocks, one for each excluded namespace, with `negate: true`
`match.any[].resources.kinds: [Deployment]` and a `preconditions` entry with operator `NotEquals` on `request.namespace`
optionNotes: Correct: `match` selects the resource kind and `exclude` removes specific namespaces; both blocks accept `any`/`all` lists with `resources`, `subjects`, `roles` and `clusterRoles` filters.
Namespace filters in `match` do not support a `!` negation prefix; listing names there only includes those namespaces.
A rule has a single `match` block and there is no `negate` field; exclusion is expressed with the dedicated `exclude` block.

`preconditions` can technically filter by `{{request.namespace}}`, but it is evaluated after matching and is meant for context-based conditions; the idiomatic and reportable way to skip namespaces is `exclude`.
explanation: Kyverno rules select resources with `match` and remove a subset with `exclude`; both support `any` (OR) and `all` (AND) lists of resource, subject, role and clusterRole filters, including `namespaces`, `names`, `selector` and `namespaceSelector`. Using `exclude` keeps intent explicit and shows correctly in `kyverno apply` and reports.
example:
spec:
  rules:
  - name: require-owner
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Deployment]
    exclude:
      any:
      - resources:
          namespaces: [kube-system, kyverno]
    validate:
      message: "owner label required"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          labels:
            owner: "?*"
diagram:
flowchart LR
    ALL["All Deployments"] --> M["match kinds Deployment"]
    M --> X{"exclude namespaces kube-system kyverno"}
    X -->|"excluded"| SKIP["Rule skipped"]
    X -->|"not excluded"| V["validate runs"]

prompt: A Kyverno validate `pattern` contains `spec: { =(hostNetwork): false }`. How does Kyverno evaluate a Pod against this pattern?
options: If `spec.hostNetwork` is present it must equal `false`; if it is absent the rule passes
`spec.hostNetwork` must be present and equal to `false`, otherwise the rule fails
If `spec.hostNetwork` is absent Kyverno adds it with value `false`
The rule only applies when `spec.hostNetwork` is present and, in that case, checks the rest of the pattern
optionNotes: Correct: `=()` is the equality anchor: it makes validation of the wrapped key conditional on its presence. An absent key is not a violation.
This is the behaviour of a plain key without any anchor; a missing `hostNetwork` would then fail because the pattern expects a value.
Adding a default is the job of the `+()` add-if-not-present anchor, which is only valid in `mutate` rules, not in `validate` patterns.
That describes the conditional anchor `()`: if the anchored key/value matches, the remaining sibling fields in the pattern are validated. The equality anchor checks the anchored key's value itself.
explanation: Kyverno anchors change how a pattern key is interpreted. `=(key)` validates the value only if the key exists, `(key)` makes the sibling fields conditional on the anchored key/value matching, `+(key)` adds the field if missing (mutate only), `^()` matches at least one list element, and `X()` negates. For `hostNetwork`, `=(hostNetwork): false` allows Pods that omit the field, which defaults to false.
example:
validate:
  message: "host namespaces are not allowed"
  pattern:
    spec:
      =(hostNetwork): false     # only checked if present
      =(hostPID): false
      =(hostIPC): false
# conditional anchor example
#    containers:
#    - (image): "*:latest"       # if image is latest ...
#      imagePullPolicy: Always   # ... then this must hold
diagram:
flowchart TD
    P["Pod spec"] --> Q{"hostNetwork present?"}
    Q -->|"no"| PASS1["pass"]
    Q -->|"yes"| V{"value false?"}
    V -->|"yes"| PASS2["pass"]
    V -->|"no"| FAIL["fail"]
    A["Anchors =() equality, () conditional, +() add-if-absent"] -.-> Q

prompt: In a Kyverno `generate` rule, what boolean field must be set to `true` so that changes to the source resource are propagated to the generated copies and generated resources are recreated if deleted?
explanation: `synchronize: true` turns a generate rule into a continuous controller: Kyverno keeps the generated resource in sync with the `data` or `clone` source, restores it if someone deletes it, and removes it when the triggering resource goes away. Without it, generation is a one-time action at creation.
example:
rules:
- name: default-deny
  match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Namespace]}}]}
  generate:
    apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    name: default-deny
    namespace: "{{request.object.metadata.name}}"
    synchronize: true          # keep in sync, recreate if deleted
    data:
      spec:
        podSelector: {}
        policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    NS["New Namespace created"] --> G["generate rule"]
    G --> NP["NetworkPolicy default-deny"]
    NP -->|"deleted by user"| G
    SRC["Source data changes"] -->|"synchronize true"| NP
    NS -->|"namespace deleted"| RM["generated resource removed"]

prompt: A Kyverno `verifyImages` rule with a cosign public key successfully verifies the signature on `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.0` during admission. Besides admitting the Pod, what does Kyverno do to the Pod by default?
options: It mutates the image reference to include the verified digest, e.g. `ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.0@sha256:...`
It adds an `imagePullSecret` for the registry to the Pod
It records the signature in a `ClusterPolicyReport` and leaves the Pod unchanged
It sets `imagePullPolicy: Always` so the tag is re-verified on every restart
optionNotes: Correct: `mutateDigest` defaults to `true`, so Kyverno rewrites the image to its immutable digest form. This guarantees the running image is exactly the one whose signature was checked, defeating tag mutation after admission.
Kyverno reads registry credentials for its own verification but does not inject pull secrets into workloads.
Verification results can appear in reports, but by default the Pod is also mutated; it is not left unchanged unless `mutateDigest: false` is set.
Kyverno does not change `imagePullPolicy`; digest pinning already makes the reference immutable.
explanation: `verifyImages` rules check signatures (cosign key, keyless, or notary) and optional attestations such as SBOMs or vulnerability scans. On success, Kyverno by default adds the digest to the image reference (`mutateDigest: true`) and, with `verifyDigest: true`, ensures a digest is present. Set `mutateDigest: false` if another controller must own the image field.
example:
rules:
- name: check-signature
  match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}]}
  verifyImages:
  - imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/acme/*"]
    mutateDigest: true        # default
    attestors:
    - entries:
      - keys:
          publicKeys: |-
            -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
            MFkw...
            -----END PUBLIC KEY-----
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["Pod image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4.0"] --> K["Kyverno verifyImages"]
    K -->|"fetch signature"| R["Registry OCI signature"]
    R -->|"cosign verify with key"| K
    K -->|"valid"| M["Mutate image to tag@sha256 digest"]
    M --> A["Pod admitted"]
    K -->|"invalid"| D["Pod rejected"]

prompt: You write a Kyverno validate rule that references `{{request.userInfo.username}}` to block Pods created by a specific user. Applying the policy fails with an error about the variable. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Background scanning is enabled by default and `request.userInfo` does not exist outside admission; set `spec.background: false`
`request.userInfo` is only available in `mutate` rules; convert the rule to a mutate rule with a `deny` patch
Variables must be referenced as `${request.userInfo.username}`; fix the variable syntax
`spec.validationFailureAction` must be `Enforce` for user-based variables; change it from `Audit`
optionNotes: Correct: `background` defaults to `true`, meaning Kyverno also applies the rule to existing resources in reports; there is no admission request in that context, so variables like `request.userInfo`, `request.operation` and `serviceAccountName` are disallowed unless `background: false`.
Admission-time variables are available to all rule types during admission; the problem is background scanning, not the rule type.
Kyverno uses JMESPath in double curly braces `{{ }}`; the syntax in the question is already correct.
`validationFailureAction` only controls blocking versus reporting and has no effect on which variables are permitted.
explanation: Kyverno policies can run in two contexts: admission and background scans that populate PolicyReports for pre-existing resources. Background mode has no `AdmissionRequest`, so policies that use request-specific variables are rejected at creation unless `spec.background: false` is set. `request.object`, `request.namespace` and context variables from ConfigMaps or API calls remain usable in background mode.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-user
spec:
  background: false            # required: uses request.userInfo
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: deny-bob
    match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Pod]}}]}
    validate:
      message: "{{request.userInfo.username}} may not create Pods"
      deny:
        conditions:
          any:
          - key: "{{request.userInfo.username}}"
            operator: Equals
            value: bob
diagram:
flowchart TD
    POL["ClusterPolicy uses request.userInfo"] --> B{"spec.background"}
    B -->|"true default"| BS["Background scan of existing resources"]
    BS --> ERR["No AdmissionRequest - policy rejected"]
    B -->|"false"| ADM["Admission only"]
    ADM --> OK["Variable resolved from request"]
    ADM -.->|"no entries for existing resources"| PR["PolicyReport"]

prompt: A ClusterPolicy in `Enforce` mode requires all containers to run as non-root. One legacy Deployment named `legacy-agent` in namespace `ops` genuinely needs root, and the platform team does not want to weaken or edit the ClusterPolicy for everyone. Which Kyverno resource is designed for this?
options: A `PolicyException` that names the policy and rule and matches the `legacy-agent` Deployment in `ops`
An annotation `kyverno.io/ignore: "true"` on the Deployment
A namespaced `Policy` in `ops` with `validationFailureAction: Audit` that overrides the ClusterPolicy
A `CleanupPolicy` that removes the PolicyReport entries for `legacy-agent`
optionNotes: Correct: `PolicyException` is a dedicated resource (kyverno.io/v2) that exempts matching resources from specific policy rules; it can be managed with RBAC and, optionally, restricted to namespaces so exceptions are auditable rather than buried in the policy.
Kyverno does not honour a generic ignore annotation; allowing one would let any user bypass policy.
Policies do not override each other; both would be evaluated and the `Enforce` ClusterPolicy would still reject the Deployment.
`CleanupPolicy` deletes Kubernetes resources on a schedule; it does not affect admission decisions.
explanation: `PolicyException` lets you carve out exemptions without touching the policy itself. It lists `policyName`/`ruleNames` in `exceptions` and a `match` block selecting the exempted resources; exceptions must be enabled in the Kyverno deployment (`--enablePolicyExceptions`) and can be limited to a namespace with `--exceptionNamespace` so only administrators can create them.
example:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v2
kind: PolicyException
metadata:
  name: legacy-agent-root
  namespace: kyverno-exceptions
spec:
  exceptions:
  - policyName: require-run-as-nonroot
    ruleNames: [run-as-non-root]
  match:
    any:
    - resources:
        kinds: [Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod]
        namespaces: [ops]
        names: ["legacy-agent*"]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    D["Deployment legacy-agent in ops"] --> K["Kyverno admission"]
    K --> CP["ClusterPolicy require-run-as-nonroot Enforce"]
    PE["PolicyException matches legacy-agent"] -->|"exempts rule"| K
    K -->|"exception applies"| OK["Admitted and reported as skip"]
    O["Other Deployments"] --> K
    K -->|"no exception"| NO["Rejected if root"]
